title: Ang 21–25: the river and the fish
hookLine: the soul as a fish in the Lord's river
tomorrow: how do you wash a mind?

cards: Senior year has a conversation that happens at every lunch table: who's staying close, who's going far. Some people can't wait to leave.

Some are quietly scared that wherever they land, they'll feel like a fish out of water. On ang twenty-five, Guru Nanak writes about a fish. And it knows something about water that the saying leaves out.

teach.h: YOU ARE THE RIVER. I AM A FISH.
teach.b: Still in Sri Rag, Mahala 1, the hymn opens in the original: tu dareeaao daanaa beenaa. You are the river, all-knowing, all-seeing. Then, in paraphrase: I am a machhulee, a little fish; how could I ever find Your end?

teach.h: WHEREVER I LOOK, THERE YOU ARE.
teach.b: And the refrain: wherever I look, there You are; pulled out of You, I burst and die.

teach.h: WHEN PAIN COMES, I CALL ON YOU.
teach.b: Then an honest line: I don't know the fisherman, and I don't know the net, but when pain comes, I call on You. And a correction: You are present everywhere; I thought You were far away.
Something to tell someone tonight: in this hymn the fish can't measure the river, and doesn't need to. It only needs to stay in it. Now take it to the lunch table.
The saying fears being pulled out of a place.
In Nanak's hymn, the river isn't a town or a house. It's the One, and the line says wherever I look, there You are.
That doesn't settle whether to stay or go; it's not that kind of hymn. It changes the question. Not where's my water, but am I still swimming in it, whatever city I wake up in?

how: Guru Nanak's hymn of the river and the fish stands in Sri Rag on ang 25; Sikhs read it in the gurdwara, at home and in a sehaj path, and sing it in kirtan.

games.q: the river hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the little fish that can't find its end
wherever I look, there You are

s: the river in the hymn is one of the rivers of Punjab
the river is the One: wherever I look, there You are.
the fish admits it calls out when pain comes
I don't know the fisherman or the net, but when pain comes, I call on You.
the hymn says a fish should find out where its river ends
the fish can't find the river's end, and doesn't need to; it needs to stay in it.

games.q: your cousin starts college across the country and texts: everything here is strange, i don't even feel like me. what does the river hymn offer him?
o: come home: the hymn says a fish pulled out of its river dies.
the river isn't a place he left: wherever he looks, it's there.
toughen up: the fish just has to learn to live on land.
games.why: in Nanak's hymn the river is the One, and the refrain says wherever I look, there You are. the question isn't where his water is, but whether he's still swimming in it.

practice: Cup your hands together in your lap as if they were holding water. Breathe slowly, and with each breath out, let your shoulders loosen the way a fish lets the current carry it.
If you have the page, read the refrain on ang twenty-five once first: wherever I look, there You are.

wordCard.voice: Ang 21. Where Sri Rag's run of hymns leads toward Guru Nanak's river and its little fish. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: machhulee, a little fish; Guru Nanak's word for the soul in the river hymn on ang 25.

carryVoice: For the road: the fish and the river, and a river that's wherever you look. Be well.
